newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan credit tightening unlikely in near term - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Japan credit tightening unlikely in near term - IMF.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is unlikely to tighten credit in the near term until the effects of the rise in the national sales tax become clear, Stanley Fischer, First Deputy Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said on Tuesday.
"It (a credit tightening) is very unlikely in the short term given the lack of information (over the effect of the tax rise)," Fischer told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Japan raised its national consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.
But Fischer also said the BOJ may raise rates in the latter half of the year if the Japanese economy continues to recover.
"If, by the third quarter, the growth is back on track, then I can see the BOJ deciding to raise interest rates later somewhere down the road," he said.
On the other hand, Fischer also said the Japanese government may be forced to take economic stimulus steps if growth slows down to the lower end of one percent for 1997.
Fischer said the current range of the dollar/yen rate was not inappropriate, but added that the speed of the yen's recent strengthening was surprising.
"That it's (dollar/yen rate) in this range now is not inappropriate, not a big surpise," Fischer said, adding: "What surprised people is how quickly it moved."

He also said many people pointed out that the dollar had gone too far when it rose to 127 yen, and said "it makes lots of sense" that it has moved back to the current range. -- George Nishiyama, Tokyo Policy Desk +81-3-5473-3710
